title: You Cannot Keep Using Your Childhood as Permission to Wound the People Who Never Caused It.
paragraphs:
You Cannot Keep Using Your Childhood as Permission to Wound the People Who Never Caused It.
Your childhood may explain why you learned to survive this way. But Jesus loves you too much to let yesterday’s wounds become tomorrow’s family inheritance.
There comes a moment in healing when the question changes.
For years, maybe the question was:
“What happened to me?”
And that question mattered.
Maybe nobody protected you when they should have.

Maybe affection in your house had conditions attached to it. Maybe silence meant someone was angry. Maybe footsteps in the hallway made your stomach tighten. Maybe you learned to study facial expressions before you were old enough to understand why.
Maybe “I love you” was rarely spoken.
Maybe “I’m sorry” was never spoken.

Maybe the adults who were supposed to make you feel safe were themselves wounded people who never learned how to love without controlling, exploding, withdrawing, manipulating, humiliating, or disappearing.
And you adapted.
You became quiet.
Or funny.
Or tough.
Or invisible.
Or hyper-independent.
You learned not to need anybody because needing people had become dangerous.
You learned to strike first because being vulnerable felt like volunteering to be wounded.
You learned to shut down during conflict because somewhere inside you, disagreement still feels like the beginning of abandonment.
You learned to raise your voice because nobody listened when you spoke softly.
You learned to control everything because chaos once controlled you.
You learned survival.
And perhaps those survival instincts helped a frightened child make it through circumstances that child never should have carried.
But now there is another question.
A harder question.
Not merely:
“What happened to me?”
But:
“What is happening to the people around me because I refuse to deal with what happened to me?”
That question hurts.
Because sometimes the child who was wounded grows into an adult who wounds.
Not intentionally at first.
Not always maliciously.
Sometimes pain simply learns our address so well that eventually it starts answering the door for us.
Someone disappoints you, and suddenly they are paying for something your father did twenty-five years ago.
Your spouse asks an innocent question, but you hear your controlling mother in their voice.
Your child makes a mistake, and something inside you erupts because mistakes were never safe when you were young.
A friend gets too close, so you push them away before they can abandon you.
Someone lovingly confronts you, and instead of hearing concern, you hear condemnation.
So you attack.
Withdraw.
Punish.
Manipulate.
Go silent.
Become cruel.
Build walls.
And eventually the people who never created your wounds begin bleeding from them.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Because Jesus does not look at your past and say, “It did not matter.”
He knows it mattered.
He sees what happened behind doors nobody else opened.
He knows every night you cried quietly.
Every moment you felt unwanted.
Every word somebody spoke over you that still echoes inside your mind.
Every betrayal.
Every absence.
Every humiliation.
Every wound you learned to hide beneath “I’m fine.”
Christ is not indifferent to wounded people.
But neither does He call us to build permanent homes inside our wounds.
The Gospel does something far more radical.
Jesus meets us in the place where we were wounded...
and begins teaching us how not to become what wounded us.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:31:
The language is piercing.
πικρία — pikria — bitterness.
θυμός — thymos — wrath, heated passion.
ὀργή — orgē — anger.
κραυγή — kraugē — clamor, the outcry of hostility.
βλασφημία — blasphēmia — abusive or slanderous speech.
And then comes the command:
ἀρθήτω — arthētō.
Let it be removed.
Taken away.
Paul does not tell wounded believers merely to become better at explaining their bitterness.
He calls them, in Christ, to put it away.
That distinction matters.
Because explanation is not transformation.
Understanding why you scream does not make screaming at your family acceptable.
Understanding why you fear abandonment does not make controlling another person acceptable.
Understanding why vulnerability frightens you does not make emotional cruelty acceptable.
Understanding why you distrust people does not give you permission to punish trustworthy people for somebody else’s betrayal.
Your history can explain your reactions without sanctifying them.
Your wounds deserve compassion.
The people being wounded by your wounds deserve compassion too.
And Scripture refuses to force us into the false choice of caring about only one.
Then Paul writes something extraordinary:
“Become kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another...”
Notice the movement.
Put this away.
Become this instead.
That is Christianity.
Not merely behavior suppression.
Transformation.
The Gospel does not simply tell the angry person, “Stop being angry.”
It brings the angry person to Christ and begins changing what anger has been producing.
It does not merely tell the hardened heart, “Stop being hard.”
It reveals the mercy of God until mercy begins flowing through places where bitterness once lived.
And Paul gives the foundation:
“...καθὼς καὶ ὁ θεὸς ἐν Χριστῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν.”
God forgave you...
in Christ.
There is the center.
Not self-improvement.
Not motivational psychology dressed in Christian vocabulary.
Christ.
You cannot heal yourself into salvation.
You cannot therapy your way into justification before God.
You cannot blame your parents into righteousness.
You cannot discipline yourself enough to erase your sin.
Our deepest problem is not merely that people sinned against us.
It is also that we have sinned against God.
Some of us were victims of terrible wrongdoing.
And later, in our own ways, we became perpetrators of wrongdoing toward others.
That truth is uncomfortable.
But the cross is where uncomfortable truth and unimaginable mercy meet.
Jesus Christ does not merely expose what others did to you.
He exposes what sin has done in all of us.
And then He does something scandalous.
He offers grace.
At the cross, Jesus does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the blood of the spotless Son of God.
Yet His love is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That means you no longer need to spend your life choosing between two prisons.
You do not have to live forever as “the victim.”
And you do not have to become “the villain.”
There is another identity available.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Being transformed.
You can say:
“Yes, they wounded me.”
And:
“Yes, I have wounded others.”
And then:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That is not weakness.
That is repentance.
Repentance is not pretending your childhood did not hurt.
Repentance is refusing to make your pain your master.
It is looking honestly at what has been passed down through your family and saying:
It stops here.
The screaming stops here.
The humiliation stops here.
The silent treatment stops here.
The manipulation stops here.
The emotional abandonment stops here.
The refusal to apologize stops here.
The addiction stops here.
The bitterness stops here.
The pretending stops here.
Not because you suddenly became strong enough.
Because Christ is making you new.
Maybe your father never apologized.
You can.
Maybe your mother never admitted when she was wrong.
You can.
Maybe nobody in your house talked about feelings without turning them into weapons.
You can learn.
Maybe your family mocked weakness.
You can become tenderhearted.
Maybe forgiveness was never modeled for you.
You have a greater model now.
“...God in Christ forgave you.”
And forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was good.
It does not require calling abuse acceptable.
It does not mean automatically restoring trust where there is continuing danger or unrepentant destructive behavior.

Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical. Biblical forgiveness releases personal vengeance into the hands of God; healthy reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and the rebuilding of trust.
Sometimes loving someone requires boundaries.
Sometimes repentance includes getting serious help.
Sometimes saying, “Jesus is healing me” needs to be accompanied by, “I need pastoral counsel,” or “I need a qualified counselor,” or “I need accountability because I keep hurting people.”
Seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
Sometimes it is one of the ways humility finally stops hiding.
Because you can know Bible verses and still need to learn how to communicate without destroying somebody.
You can worship loudly on Sunday and terrify your family on Monday.
You can post Scripture online while refusing to apologize at home.
You can know Christian language and still use silence as punishment.
You can call yourself “strong” when what you really mean is, “I am terrified of ever being vulnerable again.”
Jesus did not save us so we could become religious versions of the people who wounded us.
He came to make us new.
And perhaps somebody reading this just felt exposed.
Not condemned.
Exposed.
There is a difference.
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for you.”
Conviction says, “You cannot keep living like this. Come home.”
So come home.
You may not be able to change what happened when you were seven.
But by the grace of God, seven-year-old you does not have to keep controlling forty-year-old you.
The person who abandoned you does not deserve another twenty years of indirect control over your marriage.
The person who screamed at you does not deserve to keep speaking through your mouth to your children.
The person who made you feel worthless does not deserve to keep determining how you respond whenever somebody loves you.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not the polished version.
Bring Him the rage.
The grief.
The resentment.
The questions.
The memories you wish would disappear.
The shame over what was done to you.
And the shame over what you have done because of it.
Bring all of it.
The Gospel has room for both the wounded child you were and the responsible adult you have become.
Grace can hold both truths.
You deserved compassion for what happened to you.
And the people around you deserve a version of you that is willing to heal.
That sentence may hurt.
But sometimes the sentence that hurts is the one that finally opens the prison door.
Maybe tonight you need to walk into another room and say:
“I was wrong.”
No “but.”
No explanation disguised as an apology.
No reminder of what they did first.
Just:
“I was wrong. I hurt you. Please forgive me.”
Maybe your children need to discover that adults can repent.
Maybe your spouse needs to hear that your defensiveness was never their responsibility to carry.
Maybe somebody who has loved you patiently needs to know that you finally see the wounds your wounds have caused.
And maybe you need to hear something too.
Your worst moment does not have to become your final identity.
Peter failed.
David needed repentance.
Paul had a past stained with violence against believers.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories would have been permanently disqualified if grace only belonged to people with clean histories.
But Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing sin out of the story.
But by taking guilty, wounded, complicated human beings and writing redemption where destruction once appeared inevitable.
Maybe you inherited anger.
Jesus can teach you gentleness.
Maybe you inherited emotional distance.
Jesus can teach you love.
Maybe you inherited bitterness.
Jesus can teach you forgiveness.
Maybe you inherited dysfunction so old nobody remembers where it started.
Through Christ, you can become the person in your family where it begins to end.
Imagine that.
Your grandchildren someday living differently because you finally surrendered what your grandparents never healed.
Your children remembering:
“My parent wasn't perfect. But they apologized.”
“They changed.”
“They sought help.”
“They prayed.”
“They stopped pretending.”
“They showed me what repentance looked like.”
“They taught me that following Jesus means allowing Him to confront what is destroying us.”
That is legacy.
Not perfection.
Repentance.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two words are enough to tell another struggling believer, “I am fighting too.”
And if Christ has already been breaking a destructive pattern in your family, tell somebody below. Your testimony may become evidence of hope for a person who thinks they can never change.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Come back.
Read Ephesians 4:31–32.
Remember:
Put away bitterness.
Become tenderhearted.
Forgive because God has forgiven you in Christ.
Not as a performance.
Not so people will think you are spiritual.
If sharing truth helps one family interrupt a cycle of destruction and turn toward Christ, that matters.
Supporting Christian ministry is not what earns God's favor, proves that you love Him, or purchases spiritual blessing. Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial support.
But generosity can be one voluntary way believers participate in work they believe is bearing Gospel fruit.
And comment if God is dealing with your heart right now.
Because perhaps the greatest testimony your childhood could ever produce is not that you survived what happened to you.
Perhaps it is that, through Jesus Christ, what happened to you did not get the final word over what came through you.
The wound may explain where the story became broken.
But Jesus gets to decide where the breaking stops.
